desc: The matrix contains only 0s and 1s. Count how many square sub-blocks (of any side length, including 1 x 1) are made up entirely of 1s. Two blocks are different if they cover different cells, even when one lies inside the other.
hints: Counting the squares position by position is expensive. Instead, group squares by their bottom-right corner.
Let side[r][c] be the largest all-ones square ending at (r, c). How many squares end exactly at that corner?
If the biggest square has side k, then squares of sides 1, 2, ..., k all end at that corner. So the answer is the sum of all side[r][c], with side[r][c] = 1 + min(up, left, up-left) for 1-cells.
editorial: A square is determined by its bottom-right corner and its side. For a fixed corner (r, c), if an all-ones square of side k ends there, so does one of every smaller side, because it is a sub-block. Hence the number of squares ending at the corner equals the largest side k found there.

That largest side follows the usual recurrence side[r][c] = 1 + min(side[r-1][c], side[r][c-1], side[r-1][c-1]) for a 1-cell and 0 otherwise. Summing side over the whole matrix gives the total in O(m · n) time; two rows of storage are enough.
